pieces.title: A canon of medicine was used for six hundred years, yet its author spent his life on the road: Ibn Sina
pieces.hook: He wove scattered experience into a system others could learn: he kept moving from place to place, yet still insisted on writing medicine as a book that could be taught.
pieces.takeaway: He wove scattered experience into a system others could learn: he kept moving from place to place, yet still insisted on writing medicine as a book that could be taught.
pieces.imageAlt: A later portrait of Ibn Sina
pieces.imageCredit: Anonymous (Wellcome Collection) · CC BY 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

parts: Ibn Sina (Ibn Sina, Latin name Avicenna, 980—1037), a physician, philosopher and scientist, was born in Afshana, near Bukhara in what is now Uzbekistan. The Canon of Medicine that he wrote was later translated into Latin and remained in use at European universities into the 17th century.
He is often described as “a polymath standing in a library,” but he spent most of his own life in courts, in exile and on the road.

In 980 he was born under the Samanid dynasty. His father was an official, and the household had access to scholars of many kinds. Later biographies say that as a youth he had already read widely across several fields, and that after treating the dynasty’s ruler he was granted access to the royal library.

Such accounts carry an element of self-description and later embellishment, but one point is fairly clear: he entered the world of the court as a physician at an early age, rather than rising step by step through a university in the modern sense.

【Once the Samanid dynasty fell, he took to the road】Around 999 the Samanid dynasty collapsed. He left Bukhara and lived, in turn, in places such as Khwarezm, Gurgan, Rey, Hamadan and Isfahan. He treated different local rulers, was sometimes entrusted with ministerial duties, and was at other times imprisoned or forced to leave because of court intrigues.
Writing was often finished in the intervals of travel, duty and confinement.

paras.lead: The Canon of Medicine and The Book of Healing
parts: From about the second decade of the 11th century he began to compile the Canon of Medicine systematically, and completed it in the Hamadan area in the 1020s. The work runs to five volumes, organizing Greco-Roman medicine, Persian and Indian experience, and his own clinical observations into a system that could be searched and taught: from anatomy, pathology and drugs to discussions of particular diseases.

At almost the same time he also wrote The Book of Healing (al-Shifa), a major work of philosophy and science. After the 12th century this book entered Europe through Latin translation; the more influential versions are often linked to the translation tradition of Toledo. For later European readers, his Latin name, Avicenna, first of all meant a medical book that could be set on a university lectern.
In the Islamic world it was likewise annotated again and again, and became one of the standard texts in the training of physicians.

His medicine was built on ancient frameworks such as humoral theory, and many of his specific judgments were later overturned by experiment and dissection. The truly lasting contribution is not so much any single prescription as this: he wrote medicine as structured knowledge, stressing order in observation, diagnosis and the use of drugs.
He died in Hamadan in 1037, at about the age of 57. Accounts of the cause mention colic, overwork and the like; the details are uncertain.

critical.label: Another angle
items: Ibn Sina｜View: Both medicine and philosophy ought to be written systematically.；Stake: To obtain patronage so that he could go on researching and practicing medicine.；Concern: That court intrigues would interrupt the work.；Basis: He completed the Canon of Medicine and The Book of Healing while on the move.

Local courts｜View: A famous physician could treat the ruler and also adorn the regime.；Stake: Health, prestige and administrative talent.；Concern: That a capable man would meddle in politics.；Basis: He was appointed many times, and was also punished or forced to leave many times.

The scholarly tradition of the Islamic world｜View: Greek learning should be absorbed and carried further.；Stake: To form a body of knowledge that could be taught.；Concern: That philosophical and religious interpretations would come into conflict.；Basis: His philosophical works were widely read, and were also criticized by theologians.

Medieval European universities｜View: The Canon of Medicine was a ready-made authoritative textbook.；Stake: To have a well-structured teaching text.；Concern: That an authoritative text would long be treated as unalterable truth.；Basis: Latin translations entered the curriculum after the 12th century and were used for hundreds of years.

Modern experimental medicine｜View: Dissection, experiment and statistics must revise the ancient framework.；Stake: To build a medicine that can be falsified.；Concern: That the earlier tradition of clinical observation would be wiped out entirely.；Basis: The Canon of Medicine gradually lost its dominant place after the 17th century.

critical.label: Checks and trade-offs
items: The court gave him a living and a library; it also gave him prison and flight.
Europe respected his authority, and later had to break that same authority in order to move toward experimental medicine.
The reputation of a “polymath” helped the works spread, but it may also obscure this: he was, first of all, a man writing books inside unstable politics.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: That a book could be taught for six hundred years shows it was complete enough; it also shows that completeness can sometimes harden into an authority that is not easily corrected.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: Many of the specific stories of a youthful genius come mainly from later biographical tradition and are hard to verify item by item.
There is no reliable contemporary medical case record of the immediate cause of death.
The details of his disputes with certain contemporaries are emphasized differently in different sources.

pieces.title: Putting the patient to sleep under the knife: one hundred and eighty years of anesthesia
pieces.short: One hundred and eighty years of anesthesia
pieces.hook: On 16 October 1846, the American dentist William Morton, at Massachusetts General Hospital in Boston, used ether to put a pat…
pieces.imageAlt: Hinckley’s history painting: the first public ether operation, in 1846
pieces.imageCredit: Robert Cutler Hinckley · Public domain, Wikimedia Commons

parts: On 16 October 1846, the American dentist William Morton used ether at Massachusetts General Hospital in Boston to put a patient to sleep. Surgeons cut out a tumor in the neck, and the patient no longer screamed and struggled as before. The day later came to be called “Ether Day.”
Operations could from then on be done with more care and for longer, because an older problem had first been solved: how to make a person endure the knife.

Pain was not first noticed in the 19th century. In antiquity and the Middle Ages, wine, opium and plant preparations such as datura were used; ancient China has records of Hua Tuo’s “Mafeisan,” but its composition and effects cannot be checked by modern methods. In 1842 the physician Crawford Long had already used ether to operate on a patient, only there was at the time no public demonstration that peers could examine.
What truly changed the profession was the 1846 demonstration that put the method into a hospital theater and let many people see it at the same time.
In 1847, James Young Simpson used chloroform in obstetrics. Ether and chloroform soon reached China: ether around 1847, chloroform around 1848. Early anesthesia was not safe.

Nineteenth-century statistics showed that the risk of death with chloroform was clearly higher than with ether, and it later faded from the mainstream because of risks such as cardiac arrest. From the beginning, anesthesia was not a matter of “falling asleep is enough,” but a technique for managing breathing, circulation and dose.

paras.lead: From a gas to a discipline
parts: At the end of the 19th century, cocaine was used for local anesthesia. The 20th century brought spinal anesthesia, intravenous anesthetics, and inhalational anesthetics that could be controlled more closely. In the 1940s, muscle relaxants entered the operating room, allowing anesthesiologists to give surgeons a quieter field while they controlled the patient’s breathing.

Monitoring equipment, endotracheal intubation and postoperative resuscitation turned anesthesia from “the person who poured the ether” into an independent medical specialty. The range of surgery widened with it: operations on the chest, the heart and the microscopic scale all depended on putting a patient safely into, and then bringing the patient back from, unconsciousness.

【Where things stand now — safer, and easier to forget】In a modern hospital, anesthesia is often remembered only after a successful operation, yet it is the first thing asked about when something goes wrong. It is already quite safe, but it is never zero-risk, especially in emergencies, with a full stomach, in the very old, and where monitoring is lacking.

Pain management has also extended from the operation itself to the period after surgery and to childbirth. The aim of anesthesia is no longer only “to put a person to sleep,” but this: to lose pain and consciousness for as long as necessary, while breathing and circulation are kept, and then to let the person wake.

critical.label: Another angle
items: Anesthesiologists｜View: Freedom from pain must be managed together with the vital signs.；Stake: Professional standing and independent judgment.；Concern: Being seen as only an auxiliary role, there to “put people under.”；Basis: In the 20th century, specialization, monitoring and airway management became the standard.

Surgeons｜View: They need quiet, stable operating time that is long enough.；Stake: To complete more complex procedures.；Concern: That an anesthetic accident will interrupt the operation.；Basis: Muscle relaxation and endotracheal intubation widened the boundaries of surgery.

Patients and families｜View: There should be no pain, and the person should also be able to wake.；Stake: Less suffering, and lower risk.；Concern: Allergy, awareness during surgery, and cognitive changes afterward.；Basis: Informed consent has become routine; the risks are higher in emergencies and in high-risk groups.

Makers of drugs and equipment｜View: More controllable drugs and more precise monitoring can reduce accidents.；Stake: Hospital purchasing and replacement cycles.；Concern: That a serious adverse effect will destroy a product line.；Basis: Chloroform left the mainstream; new drugs and new machines keep entering the operating room.

Hospitals and regulators｜View: The safety of anesthesia is a measure of the quality of care.；Stake: Fewer deaths and fewer lawsuits.；Concern: Uneven provision of equipment and staff.；Basis: Modern hospitals treat preoperative assessment, intraoperative monitoring and resuscitation as a system, not merely as individual skill.

critical.label: Checks and trade-offs
items: Stronger anesthesia gives surgery more freedom, and also demands higher capacity for monitoring and rescue.
Public demonstration sped the spread; early statistics then showed that a new method can bring new ways of dying.
Patients want to “know nothing at all”; physicians must avoid going too deep, lasting too long, and being unable to reverse the state.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: The ideal state of anesthesia is to succeed so completely that people forget it; that invisibility is both its achievement and the reason it is easily pushed back in the allocation of resources.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: The composition of Hua Tuo’s Mafeisan cannot be confirmed, and it cannot simply be written as “the world’s earliest surgical anesthetic.”
The specific ratios of anesthetic mortality in the 19th century come from case compilations of different origins, and the definitions are not the same.
Contemporary anesthetic mortality varies widely by country and type of surgery; this article does not adopt an unchecked single figure of “so many deaths per ten thousand.”

pieces.title: Huang had only just left, yet revenue doubled: Nvidia’s third quarter
pieces.hook: After the U.S. market close on 17 November, Nvidia reported results for the period ended 25 October 2026…
pieces.event: 2026-11-17 released third-quarter results; 11-11 the board accepted Jensen Huang’s resignation
pieces.imageAlt: Aerial photograph of Nvidia’s Santa Clara campus

parts: After the U.S. market close on 17 November, Nvidia reported results for the third quarter of fiscal 2027, ended 25 October 2026: revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103% from $57.0 billion a year earlier, and up 20% from $96.2 billion in the previous quarter. Under U.S. generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP), net income was $65.3 billion, up 105%; diluted earnings per share were $2.70.

This was the first quarterly report the company delivered after co-founder Jensen Huang resigned on 11 November, presented by chief financial officer Colette Kress, who is also serving as interim chief executive. The company’s revenue guidance for the fourth quarter is $130.0 billion, plus or minus 3%.
Analyst expectations compiled by the London Stock Exchange Group had previously stood at $109.1 billion in revenue and $2.48 in adjusted earnings per share.

paras.lead: First, make the personnel changes clear
parts: On 11 November the board accepted Huang’s resignation as president, chief executive and director, effective immediately. Kress has been chief financial officer since 2013, and now also serves as interim chief executive until a permanent successor is named; the board said it would consider both internal and external candidates.

Director Harvey C. Jones was appointed as the company’s first chairman. A company press release on the 12th announced only these arrangements, and confirmed that earnings would be released on the 17th as planned. As for the reason for the resignation, the Associated Press and other outlets reported that it came after coverage of Huang’s personal relationships, and of national-security concerns raised in connection with them.
These accounts come from news reports, not from conclusions in the company’s press release.

paras.lead: The figures themselves are still very large
parts: Data-center revenue was $107.6 billion, up 110% year on year and 21% quarter on quarter, still the overwhelming mainstay. Edge-computing revenue was $8.2 billion, up 42% year on year. The GAAP gross margin was 74.8%, almost unchanged from 75.0% in the previous quarter, and higher than 73.4% a year earlier.

Operating income was $77.5 billion, up 115%. The company said the new Vera Rubin NVL72 system had already shipped, and was one of the fastest ramps in its history. In the third quarter the company returned $28.1 billion to shareholders in the form of buybacks and cash dividends; at the end of the quarter, about $227.3 billion remained under the repurchase authorization.
The next quarterly dividend, $0.25, will be paid on 23 December.

paras.lead: Two points in the guidance are more worth watching
parts: The fourth-quarter guidance includes an extra week. Revenue is pointed at about $130.0 billion, but both GAAP and non-GAAP gross-margin guidance are 71.0% to 72.0%, a step down from this quarter’s level near 75%.

The company stated clearly: the guidance assumes no data-center compute revenue from China. What the market can see is that “volume is still expanding,” and also that “each dollar may not be quite as thick,” as well as that an important market has not been counted into the compute business.

【The share price fell first and then bounced, but that was not the closing price】In regular trading in New York on the 17th, Nvidia closed at $155.46, down 0.44%. According to Yahoo Finance, after the earnings release, at about 5:22 p.m., the after-hours price once reached $158.33, a rise of about 1.85%; different outlets put the after-hours gain at roughly 2%.

Trading volume was clearly higher than the recent daily average. The 52-week range was between $148.80 and $243.37, which shows that even after the after-hours rebound, the stock remained far from its high of the past year. These are trading reactions, not a guarantee for the next quarter.

paras.lead: Who benefits, who is under pressure
parts: Those lifted in the short run are cloud firms and artificial-intelligence companies still waiting for shipments: both the deliveries and the guidance say that supply is still moving forward. Shareholders saw buybacks, a dividend, and a revenue outlook above previous expectations. Under pressure is the interim leadership — Kress has to serve as finance chief and as the person in charge at the same time, and the board is still looking for a permanent appointment.

The downward revision of the gross margin, and the decision to count China compute revenue as zero, are a reminder: strong demand does not mean that every market, or the margin of every quarter, will follow the same slope.

【Keep “still growing” and “a change at the top” apart】This earnings report can be read as “the person has left, the machine is still running”; it can also be read as “growth is still there, but gross-margin guidance has already turned, and an important market has been left out of the assumptions.” Both readings use the same set of numbers.

What is missing is time: a permanent chief executive has not yet appeared, and the revenue already completed in this quarter cannot automatically answer how the next person in charge will lead the company.

critical.label: Another angle
items: The interim leadership and the board｜View: Growth comes from a continuing product cadence and from employees’ innovation; Kress is serving as both interim chief executive and finance chief, and the board is searching for a permanent successor.；Stake: To steady customers and the capital markets, complete the handover, and keep executing the published product roadmap.；Concern: That the founder’s sudden absence will weaken outside confidence; that one person holding two roles will be hard to sustain for long.；Basis: The company’s 12 November press release and 17 November earnings: Kress’s public remarks, the search for a permanent successor, and the figures on revenue, shipments and buybacks.

Investors and analysts｜View: They read the better-than-expected revenue and fourth-quarter guidance as a sign that demand is still there, while also watching the downward revision of the gross margin and the assumptions about the China business.；Stake: The share price, buybacks and dividends; on the 17th the stock closed at $155.46 and later recovered for a time after hours.；Concern: That if growth slows, margins keep falling, or the handover drags on, the valuation will come under pressure again.；Basis: The London Stock Exchange Group’s compilation of expectations; closing and after-hours prices recorded by Yahoo Finance and The Motley Fool; the 52-week range of $148.80–$243.37.

Cloud firms and large customers｜View: Computing power is still tight; the key is whether new systems arrive on schedule, and whether the software and the ecosystem remain continuous.；Stake: To obtain new platforms such as Vera Rubin, in order to support training and inference loads.；Concern: That supply will fluctuate during the handover, or that the product roadmap will be disrupted.；Basis: The earnings report said NVL72 had already shipped to partners including CoreWeave, Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure and Oracle.

Competitors and the supply chain｜View: Nvidia’s guidance is often treated as a weathervane for the whole artificial-intelligence hardware chain.；Stake: Visibility of orders; production planning at foundries, packaging houses and component suppliers.；Concern: That if the demand narrative wavers, or Nvidia’s own share shifts, related orders will swing with it.；Basis: Yahoo Finance and other reports noted that after hours on the 17th, AMD, Broadcom, TSMC and others moved in tandem with Nvidia’s results.

The policy setting and restrictions on sales to China｜View: Sales of high-end data-center compute into some markets are constrained by export controls.；Stake: To manage uncertainty in one of the largest markets, within the bounds of compliance.；Concern: That writing “this quarter still grew sharply” as “every market is already open” would conceal a clear assumption in the guidance.；Basis: In its fourth-quarter outlook the company stated clearly: it assumes no data-center compute revenue from China.

critical.label: Checks and trade-offs
items: Revenue and guidance are still expanding, yet gross-margin guidance has come down from nearly 75% this quarter to 71%—72%: volume and margin need not move in the same direction.
Buybacks and dividends are returning cash to shareholders, while the board at the same time has to rebuild the top job.
Customers care about whether the chips arrive on time; investors care about whether the handover will change that supply story.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: A strong quarter that is already finished cannot answer who the permanent chief executive will be, how the China compute business will be booked, or whether the downward revision of the gross margin is temporary or a new normal. Those questions depend on the next few quarters and on personnel announcements, not on a few percentage points after hours on the 17th.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: The specific details of the reason for the resignation come mainly from reporting by the Associated Press, The New York Times and other outlets; the company’s press release did not address them, and this article does not treat the reporting as a settled fact.
On 13 November, NBC News, citing sources, said an investigation led by independent directors was still under way; this was not a matter confirmed by the company in its 17 November earnings report.

After-hours prices move with time, and the moments and percentage changes recorded by different outlets are not entirely the same; the regular-session close of $155.46 should be treated as the figure that can be checked.

Vera Rubin’s specific contribution to revenue, and how much of the gross-margin revision comes from product mix, pricing or costs, are not broken out in numbers that can be read directly from the earnings report.

pieces.title: The Student List has entered parliament, and a government must still be formed within ninety days: a new page for Serbia
pieces.hook: On 17 November, Serbia’s 15th National Assembly held its first sitting in Belgrade: it confirmed all 2…
pieces.event: 2026-11-17 the new parliament held its first sitting and was formally constituted; the speaker election was postponed to the 18th
pieces.imageAlt: The building of Serbia’s National Assembly in Belgrade

parts: On 17 November, Serbia’s 15th National Assembly held its first sitting in Belgrade: it confirmed the credentials of all 250 members and swore them in, and the new parliament was formally constituted. This was a crucial step after the early parliamentary elections of 25 October.

According to the final results as relayed by Xinhua, “Student List – Students Are Winning” obtained 140 seats; “Aleksandar Vučić – United Serbia,” led by the Serbian Progressive Party, obtained 103 seats; five minority lists together obtained 7 seats. Candidates for speaker had already been put forward: the Student List nominated Aleksandar Čupić, and the Progressive Party side nominated Stojan Radenović.

On the 17th there was only debate, and no vote; the sitting was adjourned until 10:00 local time on the 18th. At the time of writing, a speaker had not yet been chosen, and a new government had not yet been formed.

The spark was the collapse of a railway-station canopy in Novi Sad two years ago, which killed 16 people. Students pointed to long-standing corruption, and for about two years kept up protests against the Progressive Party and its leader, then-president Vučić. On 27 September, Vučić resigned as president, and Assembly speaker Ana Brnabić began exercising the powers of the presidency.

After the vote on 25 October, a repeat vote was held at 53 polling stations on 1 November; on 5 November the Republic Electoral Commission announced the final results. The Student List obtained 2,354,417 votes, or 53.01% of all ballots; United Serbia obtained 1,731,323 votes, or 38.98%.
Turnout was 68.89% — 4,444,310 of the 6,451,292 registered voters took part, higher than 58.77% in 2023.

【The majority is already enough; time is not generous】140 seats are 14 more than the 126 needed for a majority, so the Student List does not have to find a coalition partner in order to elect a government; but it is still 27 seats short of the two-thirds (167 seats) required to amend the constitution. The constitution requires that a new government be elected within 90 days of the parliament’s being constituted; otherwise the parliament is dissolved and a new general election is held.

The newly elected speaker will take over from Brnabić in exercising the powers of the presidency, and will set the date of the presidential election. Xinhua, citing the law, said the presidential election must be held by the end of December. The new majority has to form a cabinet and, at the same time, enter the countdown to a presidential election.

paras.lead: Friction was already visible on the first day
parts: Vučić now appears in parliament as the leader of the opposition. According to Xinhua, he congratulated the new parliamentary majority and said his party group would not obstruct the working of the parliament or the forming of institutions. According to The Guardian, he also spoke in parliament for more than 90 minutes; Ilija Srdanović, a cardiologist who stood first on the Student List’s candidate list, criticized delay itself as adding to the public burden.

The election of the speaker was postponed to the 18th, and it cannot yet be written that either side has already “won the speakership.” Outside parliament there were celebrations by supporters, and there was also an incident in which yogurt was thrown at a Progressive Party member; the student movement then said this did not accord with the peace and dignity it advocates.
Vučić, for his part, used the episode to criticize.

paras.lead: A narrative frame to watch for
parts: One telling would write “the Student List has already been sworn in” as “Serbia has already entered a new era of government,” yet a cabinet has not been formed, and a president has still to be elected separately. Another would write an isolated clash as the essence of the whole movement, even though the movement itself has already publicly condemned it.

To treat Vučić’s statement that he would “not obstruct” as meaning that the transfer of power has already gone smoothly is also inaccurate for now. The 90-day clock has already started; the outcome will depend on whether parliament can elect a government within the time limit, and on how the presidential election is arranged.

critical.label: Another angle
items: The Student List and its supporters｜View: Two years of protest have produced a parliamentary majority; the next step should be to form institutions quickly and begin to govern.；Stake: To turn the demand for an end to corruption into a government that can function, and to hold on to a hard-won majority.；Concern: A lack of governing experience; that procedure will be delayed; that isolated clashes will be used to discredit the whole movement.；Basis: The Electoral Commission’s final result of 140 seats; The Guardian recorded celebrations outside parliament, and the student movement’s condemnation of the yogurt-throwing incident; Srdanović publicly complained about delay.

Vučić and United Serbia｜View: Accept the election result, while continuing to speak as the largest opposition party, and criticize attacks on Progressive Party figures.；Stake: To keep a political presence, and to influence the speaker election, the pace of cabinet-forming, and the coming presidential election.；Concern: Being marginalized after losing executive power, or being damaged further under pressure for accountability from the new majority.；Basis: Xinhua: Vučić congratulated the new majority and said he would not obstruct; The Guardian: he spoke in parliament for more than 90 minutes and criticized the clash outside.

The new parliamentary majority and a future government｜View: With a majority of seats on its own, it need not find a coalition partner in order to elect a government.；Stake: To complete the forming of a cabinet within 90 days, and to get the speaker and the presidential election timetable in order.；Concern: That if a government is not elected in time, parliament will be dissolved; the seat total is also not enough to amend the constitution alone.；Basis: Seat arithmetic as relayed by election-monitoring organizations: 140 is 14 more than 126, and 27 short of the 167-seat threshold for constitutional change; the 90-day limit in the constitution.

The acting president, the new speaker and the voters｜View: The new speaker will take over from Brnabić in exercising the powers of the presidency, and will set the date of the presidential election.；Stake: To complete, as the law requires, an election after a vacancy at the head of state, and to avoid a prolonged vacuum of authority.；Concern: That once parliamentary procedure is delayed, the time available to prepare the presidential election will be squeezed.；Basis: After Vučić resigned on 27 September, Brnabić began exercising the powers of the presidency; Xinhua said the presidential election must be held by the end of December.

Outside observers and relations with neighboring countries and the European Union｜View: The new majority has not only to handle accountability and governance at home, but also to face regional and European relations that have been strained in recent years.；Stake: To watch whether Serbia’s politics can make a stable transition, and whether foreign policy will be adjusted.；Concern: Treating “parliament has already been constituted” as meaning that foreign relations have already been rewritten is, for now, without a basis.；Basis: Al Jazeera and other reports noted that observers believe the new leadership will need to rebuild sustainable cooperation with neighbors and the European Union; specific policies have not yet been announced.

critical.label: Checks and trade-offs
items: The Student List has the seats to form a government on its own, yet it must complete the forming of a cabinet within 90 days, and at the same time enter the countdown to a presidential election.
Vučić verbally promised not to obstruct, and also made a long speech on the first day; the new majority criticized delay, and the two sides do not agree on what “normal deliberation” means.
Celebrations and clashes appeared together outside parliament: supporters want the new majority to start work, while supporters of the old authorities seize on the clashes to make a case.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: Parliament has already been constituted, but the speaker, the acting-president arrangement, a new government and the presidential election have not yet been put in place. Winning a majority of seats is not the same as having begun to govern, still less the same as having turned the page on the head of state.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: At the time of writing the speaker election had not yet been put to a vote, so neither side can be written as already having been elected speaker.
A prime minister and the Student List’s specific plan for forming a cabinet have not yet appeared in public reporting as a final list that can be checked.

The wording that the presidential election “must be held by the end of December” is quoted from Xinhua’s summary of the law; the precise deadline must follow constitutional calculation and later official decrees.

The line between “delay” and “normal debate” in the first day’s sitting is drawn differently by the two sides; this article only sets their statements side by side, and does not rule on who is obstructing.
